title: Warm winters delay cherry bloom at warm sites in Japan and Korea; a fixed thermal-time model explains the Swiss drop in spring sensitivity but not the Japanese rise (1951-2023)
abstract: Question: does the apparent drop of spring-phenology temperature sensitivity under warming need a physiological cause (chilling deficit), or does a model with constant physiology explain it? Approach: we used cherry bloom records from three independent networks: Japan (JMA, Somei-yoshino clone, 76 sites, 1953-2021, station monthly temperatures), Switzerland (MeteoSwiss, Prunus avium, 116 sites, 1951-2023, E-OBS daily) and South Korea (KMA, 58 sites, 1980-2020, ERA5 daily). We fitted a forcing-only thermal-time model (M1) on years up to 1987 only, simulated bloom dates for all years, and applied the same within-site sensitivity regression to observed and simulated dates. Intervals are 95 % site-cluster bootstrap intervals. Results: in Switzerland the sensitivity to 60-day preseason temperature dropped from -5.93 to -5.39 d/degC after 1988; M1 predicts an equal or larger drop (excess -0.14 [-0.46, 0.18] d/degC). In Japan the sensitivity rose from -3.33 to -4.28 d/degC while M1 predicts no change (excess -1.03 [-1.22, -0.85]); the rise remains in the 45 sites with continuous records, and models with chilling terms do not reproduce it. With spring temperature held constant, a warmer December-January delays bloom at sites with mild winters: +2.21 [2.01, 2.37] d/degC at the warmest Japanese sites (+1.60 before 1988, +3.25 after), +1.07 [0.53, 1.61] in Korea, +0.21 [0.02, 0.39] in cold-winter Switzerland. The delay increases with site winter temperature in all three networks; M1 dates show no such pattern. Chilling terms fitted before 1988 reduce later prediction error only at the warmest third of the Japanese sites. Limitations: Japanese temperatures are monthly and not homogenized; Korean records are short; chilling models are simple; the Japanese rise of sensitivity is not explained. No air-pollution data were used.
